newsitem.title: POLAND: Poles and Germans suggest regulating flood river.
newsitem.headline: Poles and Germans suggest regulating flood river.

text.p: German and Polish officials on Thursday proposed a joint programme with Czech and EU participation to regulate the River Oder, which has ravaged parts of all three countries with floods in the past month.

Polish Interior Minister Leszek Miller and Manfred Stolpe, the premier of Germany's neighbouring Brandenburg state, told journalists after a meeting in Warsaw that the European Union had expressed interest.

"The plan would encompass various goals -- the Oder River as a transport route, environment protection, water retention reservoirs, polders and dams which would protect cities along the river," Miller said.
"There is a chance for a European-scale project for the Oder," Stolpe said, adding that he had received a positive reaction from the EU.
Neither man gave any details of the potential investment, financing or timing of the project. Stolpe, visiting Poland for two days, also discussed the programme with Finance Minister Marek Belka.

Poland and the Czech Republic have borne the brunt of several weeks of floods which have killed more than 100 people, inundated the Polish provincial capitals of Wroclaw and Opole and forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of people.

On Thursday the Polish border town of Slubice, across the river from Germany's Frankfurt an der Oder, was maintaining a virtual ban on car traffic for the third day in a row. It was feared that vibrations could cause its sodden dikes to burst and submerge it under five metres (16 feet) of water.

"Soldiers and volunteers, who continue to heroically fight to keep the dike from cracking, have to carry sandbags about 100 metres (yards) on their backs because delivery vehicles can't approach any closer," said Marek Sobczak of the government's crisis committee.

The Oder had subsided about two cm (one inch) in 24 hours in Slubice, but remained dangerously high at 2.5 metres above alarm levels, just as it did in many other towns througout flood-hit southern and western Poland, Sobczak said.

On the German side, thousands of soldiers were laying down five-tonne sandbags to prevent a damaged dike near Hohenwutzen bursting open and unleashing a catastrophic flood over 250 sq km (95 sq miles).

The Polish weather institute said it expected light rain in the affected areas of the country area on Thursday with heavier rain in central regions on Friday, but that this was not likely to cause new flooding.
Saturday was likely to bring more light showers in the south, with a possibility of thunderstorms.
Sobczak said that in the previous 24 hours, floods had covered another 840 hectares (2,070 acres) of land but receded from more than 6,500 hectares.
Flood waters still covered nearly 1,900 square km (730 sq miles) of Poland. Of 162,000 people evacuated over the last three weeks, nearly 50,000 were still homeless.
The government has begun the massive task of reconstruction in the affected areas and the finance ministry wants to introduce a special flood tax next year to help finance the rebuilding.

Opposition parties have strongly criticised the ruling coalition of ex-communists and peasants for the way they have handled the flood crisis. The latest opinion polls show the coalition losing popularity as a result of the disaster with less than two months to go to parliamentary elections.
